panels.title: CPU per component
panels.description: The whole reason each of these has a node to itself. On the previous topology the orchestrator sat at 11% of a core and looked idle — it was sharing two shared vCPUs with the broker. Read this against the limits panel below, not on its own.

panels.title: CPU throttling
panels.description: Fraction of periods in which the kernel stopped the container because it had spent its quota. Read this as a rate over a window — the raw counters are cumulative, and dividing two lifetime totals once reports a number that means nothing.

targets.expr: sum by (pod) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total{namespace="ec-demo1", container!=""}[5m])) / clamp_min(sum by (pod) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total{namespace="ec-demo1", container!=""}[5m])), 1)

panels.title: Memory per component
panels.description: Working set, against the container limit. A JVM that plateaus just under its limit is not comfortable — it is collecting hard to stay there.

panels.title: Node CPU
panels.description: Per node, so the separation can be checked rather than assumed: postgres, orchestrator and worker each have a node to themselves, and if two of these lines move together something has been packed where it should not be.

panels.title: The database, which is usually the ceiling
JDBC pool
panels.description: Threads waiting for a connection is the number that matters — active-vs-idle only says how busy the pool is, while pending says the application is blocked on it. Zero pending with slow throughput means the bottleneck is somewhere else entirely.

panels.title: JVM garbage collection
panels.description: Seconds of pause per second. A CPU that looks busy while this is high is not doing your work; a CPU that looks idle while throughput is poor is waiting on something, and this panel is how you rule GC out in one glance.
